subject: physiology
title: Physiological Shunt, the A-a Gradient, and West Zones

steps.tx: A physiological shunt occurs when deoxygenated mixed venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli and enters the arterial system unchanged, producing hypoxaemia. The total **physiological shunt fraction** combines anatomical shunts (such as bronchial veins and thebesian veins draining to left heart chambers) with intrapulmonary pathological shunts.
steps.say: A physiological shunt occurs when venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli to enter arterial circulation, worsening hypoxaemia.

left.title: Anatomical Shunts
points: Normal physiological bypass in all healthy humans
Bronchial venous drainage into pulmonary veins
Thebesian veins draining directly into left ventricle
Accounts for normal baseline shunt fraction of 2% to 5%

right.title: Pathological Intrapulmonary Shunts
points: Seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, atelectasis
Refractory hypoxaemia unresponsive to 100% supplemental oxygen
Requires mechanical alveolar recruitment via positive end-expiratory pressure

steps.tx: The cardinal hallmark distinguishing true right-to-left shunting from simple ventilation-perfusion mismatch is the diagnostic response to supplemental hundred percent oxygen. Because shunted blood completely bypasses gas-exchanging alveolar surfaces, true **intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting** fails to correct arterial oxygen tension with pure oxygen therapy.
steps.say: True right-to-left shunts fail to correct with one hundred percent oxygen, because the shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas.

left.title: V/Q Mismatch (e.g., COPD, Asthma)
points: Low V/Q units with sluggish ventilation
Arterial PO2 readily corrects with 100% O2
High inspired PO2 overcomes poor ventilation

right.title: True Shunt (e.g., ARDS, Atelectasis, VSD)
points: V/Q ratio equals absolute zero in affected units
Deoxygenated blood completely bypasses alveolar contact
Requires positive end-expiratory pressure to recruit alveoli

steps.tx: To localize the physiological cause of arterial hypoxaemia, clinicians calculate the difference between ideal alveolar oxygen tension and measured arterial oxygen tension, designated the **alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient**. In a healthy young adult breathing room air at sea level, the normal A-a gradient is under ten to fifteen millimetres of mercury.
steps.say: The alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient helps pinpoint the cause of hypoxaemia, normally measuring under fifteen millimetres of mercury.

nodes.label: Compute Ideal PAO2 via Alveolar Gas Equation; Measure PaO2 via ABG
A-a Gradient = PAO2 - PaO2 (Normal Young Adult: 5 to 15 mmHg)
Age-Adjusted Normal Upper Limit: (Age in Years / 4) + 4
Elevated Gradient Signifies V/Q Mismatch, Shunt, or Diffusion Impairment

steps.tx: An elevated A-a gradient definitively isolates hypoxaemia to intrinsic pulmonary pathology, including ventilation-perfusion mismatch, right-to-left shunting, or impaired diffusion capacity. Conversely, hypoxaemia with a strictly **normal A-a gradient** occurs only in two specific clinical circumstances: environmental high altitude with reduced inspired oxygen, and pure central alveolar hypoventilation.
steps.say: A normal A-a gradient in a hypoxaemic patient points exclusively to central hypoventilation or low environmental oxygen.

steps.tx: Unlike systemic arterioles which dilate during regional tissue hypoxia, pulmonary arterioles exhibit an intrinsic, unique physiological reaction termed **hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction**. When local alveolar oxygen tension falls below seventy millimetres of mercury, surrounding precapillary pulmonary smooth muscle cells constrict, diverting perfusion away from underventilated hypoxic alveoli.
steps.say: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood flow away from hypoxic alveoli to preserve overall ventilation-perfusion matching.

nodes.label: Local Alveolar Hypoxia (PAO2 < 70 mmHg) Inhibits Voltage-Gated K+ Channels
Depolarization of Pulmonary Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells; Ca2+ Influx
Precapillary Arteriolar Vasoconstriction in Poorly Ventilated Lung Zones
Redistribution of Pulmonary Perfusion Toward Well-Ventilated Alveoli

steps.tx: While localized hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction beneficially optimizes global ventilation-perfusion matching, generalized chronic alveolar hypoxia causes diffuse arteriolar constriction throughout the pulmonary bed. This marked increase in pulmonary vascular resistance leads inexorably to **pulmonary arterial hypertension** and secondary right ventricular hypertrophy, known clinically as cor pulmonale.
steps.say: Generalized alveolar hypoxia triggers diffuse arteriolar constriction, causing pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy.

steps.tx: Pulmonary blood flow distribution is modeled by the classic **West zones of the lung**, dictated by interactions between pulmonary arterial pressure, alveolar gas pressure, and pulmonary venous pressure. In Zone 1 at the apex, alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure, collapsing capillaries and creating non-perfused alveolar dead space.
steps.say: The West zones explain pulmonary perfusion. In Zone 1, alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure, collapsing capillaries into dead space.

rows: Only in hypovolaemic shock or high PEEP ventilation
Waterfall effect; flow driven by (Pa - PA)
Maximal perfusion at gravity-dependent lung base
Occurs in severe pulmonary venous congestion and oedema

steps.tx: Not every breath reaches blood, and the wasted fraction has a name and a measurement. **Ventilatory dead space** is gas moved into airways and unperfused alveoli that takes no part in exchange, rising in pulmonary embolism and low cardiac output. It is estimated from expired carbon dioxide against the arterial value. A widening gap between the two in a breathless patient is the physiology of a clot stated numerically.
steps.say: Dead space is ventilation reaching no perfusion, rising in embolism and low output. The arterial to expired carbon dioxide gap measures it.

vis.alt: Image showing ventilatory dead space in unperfused alveoli of the lung.
vis.caption: Ventilated but unperfused alveoli are shown wasting inspired air. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Under normal upright resting conditions, Zone 1 is virtually absent because pulmonary arterial pressure is sufficient to perfuse the lung apex. However, when arterial pressure falls during hypovolaemic shock or alveolar pressure is artificially raised by positive-pressure mechanical ventilation, Zone 1 expands, generating massive **ventilatory dead space**.
steps.say: Zone 1 expands during hypovolaemic shock or positive-pressure ventilation, creating extensive dead space that impairs gas exchange.
